At FitWit fitness boot camp, participants take part in structured workouts. “We wanted to connect with teenagers in a way that mattered, and we saw directly that fitness and physical activity are often being ignored among this age group. The program is a six-week, after-school boot camp contest. Students earn prizes when they reach fitness targets. In one recent session involving Atlanta Public Schools students, the top prize for completing the program was an iPod Nano.

Students chosen for the competition are those who want to improve their fitness but are not already participating on an organized sports team. Participants are also given two workouts to complete at home between group sessions.

“By the end of six weeks, every participant has improved overall fitness. In our first program last spring, the average improvement in total fitness was more than 40 percent. It’s not unusual for someone to double their fitness level,” Thoele said.

“Many of these kids don’t know how to exercise, or even realize that they are capable of exercising. They begin to value pushing themselves, and when that happens, we see a huge rise in their confidence,” he added.

The CDC says obesity raises teens’ chances of developing heart disease, bone and joint issues, sleep apnea, and social and emotional difficulties.

**Atlanta nonprofit uses fitness boot camp to help teens build healthier habits**

**ATLANTA** — On a weekday afternoon in Atlanta, a group of teenagers sprint across a gym floor, drop into pushups and cheer one another through a final set of squats. The workout is tough by design — but the goal, instructors say, is bigger than burning calories.

The FitWit Foundation, an Atlanta-based nonprofit, is running a six-week fitness boot camp for teens aimed at combating childhood obesity and helping young people develop confidence, discipline and long-term healthy habits.

“We’re not just trying to get kids to exercise for six weeks,” said instructor Ben Thoele. “We’re trying to show them that fitness can be fun, that they’re capable of doing hard things and that taking care of their bodies matters.”

The program combines high-energy workouts with nutrition education, goal-setting and teamwork. Participants meet several times a week for circuit-style training that includes running, bodyweight exercises, agility drills and strength movements scaled to each teen’s ability level. Coaches also talk with students about making healthier food choices, staying active outside class and supporting one another.

The effort comes as childhood obesity remains a major public health concern. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 1 in 5 children and adolescents in the United States has obesity. CDC data from 2017 to 2020 show the prevalence of obesity was 19.7% among children and adolescents ages 2 to 19 — affecting roughly 14.7 million young people.

Health experts say obesity in childhood can increase the risk of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, breathing problems and mental health challenges. It can also make it more likely that a child will have obesity as an adult.

FitWit Foundation leaders say the boot camp is designed to meet teens where they are, especially those who may not have access to organized sports, gym memberships or consistent fitness opportunities.

“A lot of our kids come in thinking, ‘I’m not athletic,’ or ‘This isn’t for me,’” Thoele said. “By the end, they realize progress is personal. If they can do one more pushup, run a little farther or encourage someone else, that’s a win.”

For participants, the program can be both physically challenging and emotionally rewarding.

“At first, I didn’t think I could keep up,” said one teen participant. “But the coaches kept pushing me and everybody was cheering. Now I feel stronger, and I want to keep working out even after the program ends.”

The six-week session ends with a fitness challenge where teens can see how much they’ve improved since the first day. Organizers say the final test is less about competition and more about recognizing growth.

Thoele said that transformation often shows up in more than just workout results.

“You see kids stand taller,” he said. “They start believing in themselves. That’s the part that sticks.”

The FitWit Foundation says it hopes to continue expanding access to fitness and wellness programs for Atlanta-area youth, giving more teens the tools to lead healthier lives long after boot camp is over.

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- Three afternoons a week, the gym at a public middle school on Atlanta’s west side fills with the sounds of squeaking sneakers, jump ropes snapping against the floor and teenagers cheering one another through sit-ups, relay races and laps around the basketball court.

The students are part of an after-school fitness program designed to help Atlanta public school students build healthier habits through exercise, nutrition lessons and friendly competition. Modeled loosely on the weight-loss reality show “The Biggest Loser,” the program emphasizes teamwork, goal-setting and measurable improvements in health rather than dramatic weigh-ins.

Organizers say the idea is simple: give students a structured, supportive place to move more, learn how food affects their bodies and celebrate progress.

“We’re not here to embarrass anybody or put kids on a scale in front of their friends,” said one program coordinator. “We’re here to help them feel stronger, make better choices and understand that health is something they can work on every day.”

Students begin each session with warmups and stretching before rotating through fitness stations that may include cardio drills, resistance bands, dance workouts, basketball conditioning and body-weight exercises. On other days, they learn how to read nutrition labels, compare sugar content in drinks or prepare simple snacks such as fruit-and-yogurt parfaits, turkey wraps and trail mix.

The program also includes incentives. Students earn points for attendance, effort, teamwork and meeting personal goals. Prizes can include athletic shoes, water bottles, sports equipment, gift cards and tickets to local events. Organizers say the rewards help keep students motivated, but the biggest payoff has been confidence.

Some participants say they joined because they wanted to lose weight. Others came because friends signed up, or because they needed something positive to do after school. Many say they have noticed changes beyond the gym.

“I can run longer now,” said one eighth-grader. “At first I got tired really fast. Now I don’t stop as much, and I feel better in PE.”

Another student said the nutrition lessons changed what she buys at the corner store after school. “I used to get chips and soda every day,” she said. “Now sometimes I get water and a granola bar, or I wait until I get home.”

Health advocates say programs like this can be especially important in communities where students may have limited access to safe outdoor spaces, affordable sports leagues or fresh food. Childhood and teen obesity remain major public health concerns nationwide, and doctors warn that poor nutrition and inactivity can increase the risk of high blood pressure, diabetes and other health problems later in life.

But organizers say they are careful not to frame the program only around weight. Students may track changes such as stamina, flexibility, resting heart rate or the number of pushups they can complete. The focus, they say, is improvement.

“We want them to see success in different ways,” a coach said. “Maybe a student doesn’t lose many pounds, but they can run a mile faster, they’re drinking more water, they’re sleeping better and they’re proud of themselves. That matters.”

Parents have also been invited to participate through family fitness nights and take-home nutrition challenges. In some cases, students are bringing lessons back to their households, asking for more vegetables at dinner or encouraging relatives to walk with them on weekends.

School staff say they have seen benefits in the classroom as well. Students who regularly attend the program appear more energetic and engaged, and some have shown improved attendance. While organizers are still collecting data, early indicators suggest participants are making measurable gains in endurance and overall fitness.

The program’s competitive format borrows some of the excitement of reality television, but its leaders say the message is intentionally different. There are no eliminations. Students are not judged against one another. Teams win by showing consistency, encouraging classmates and making healthy choices.

At the end of each session, participants gather in a circle to talk about what went well and set goals for the next meeting. Some goals are small: drink one fewer soda, walk 15 minutes, try a new vegetable. Others are bigger: make a school team, lower a blood pressure reading, or feel comfortable exercising in front of peers.

For many students, the program has become more than an after-school activity. It is a place where fitness feels less like punishment and more like possibility.

“I thought it was going to be all about losing weight,” one student said after finishing a circuit workout. “But it’s really about getting stronger. And now I know I can.”

## Atlanta Boot Camp Helps Teens Take Steps Toward Healthier Futures

The program is FitWit, a fitness boot camp that brings together adult volunteers and teens for six weeks of exercise, encouragement and goal-setting. But FitWit volunteers stay close by, demonstrating movements, offering modifications and celebrating small victories.

Over the course of the six-week boot camp, however, she began to notice changes—not just in her stamina, but in her attitude.

With volunteers encouraging her to keep going, Raquel learned that progress did not have to mean being the fastest or strongest person in the group. Sometimes it meant finishing a workout she might have quit two weeks earlier. Sometimes it meant showing up even when she was tired. By the end of the program, her effort stood out.

To add a little extra motivation, FitWit offered an iPod Nano as a prize, giving students another reason to push themselves and stay committed through the full six weeks. But organizers and volunteers say the real rewards are bigger than any gadget: improved fitness, stronger self-esteem and a better understanding of how regular physical activity can affect long-term health.

Programs like FitWit come at a time when teen obesity remains a serious national problem. Across the United States, many adolescents struggle with weight-related health risks, often linked to a combination of limited physical activity, poor nutrition, stress and environments that make healthy choices difficult. Health experts warn that obesity in adolescence can increase the risk of diabetes, high blood pressure and other chronic conditions later in life.

That is why community-based efforts can matter. FitWit does not promise an instant transformation. Instead, it gives teenagers a structured place to move, sweat and be supported by adults who believe in them. The volunteers serve not only as fitness coaches, but also as mentors—showing students that healthy change is possible one workout at a time.

By the end of the boot camp, the teens have done more than complete six weeks of exercise. They have built friendships, tested their limits and learned that fitness is not only about appearance or competition. It is about strength, energy, discipline and feeling capable.

For Raquel and her classmates, the final workout is not an ending. It is a starting line.

**ANCHOR:**  
Childhood obesity remains one of the most serious public health challenges in the United States. According to the **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention**, about **1 in 5 children and adolescents ages 2 to 19** has obesity — that’s roughly **14.7 million young people**. The CDC also reports that obesity rates are especially high among teens, with adolescents ages 12 to 19 among the most affected.

The nonprofit teaches teens the basics of nutrition and exercise through a competitive fitness boot camp, combining workouts with lessons on food choices, goal-setting and confidence.

“We don’t want teens to think health is only about a number on a scale,” said a FitWit Foundation coach. “We want them to understand strength, energy, discipline and how daily choices add up.”

The CDC says childhood obesity can raise the risk of serious health problems, including **high blood pressure, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, breathing problems such as asthma and sleep apnea, and joint issues**. Children with obesity are also more likely to experience anxiety, depression, low self-esteem and bullying.

For many teens in the program, the appeal is the competition.

“It feels like a game, but you’re working hard the whole time,” said one teen participant. “At first I didn’t think I could keep up. Now I’m faster, and I actually like exercising.”

“Competition gives them a reason to show up,” said another instructor. “But the bigger win is when a student says, ‘I tried a vegetable I never liked before,’ or ‘I went for a walk instead of sitting on my phone all afternoon.’”

“Childhood obesity is not about blaming children or parents,” said a public health specialist. “It’s about understanding the environment kids are growing up in — what foods are affordable, whether they have safe places to play, and how much support they have at school and at home.”

For teens in the FitWit Foundation program, the boot camp can be a first step toward that daily movement.

“I used to get tired just walking up stairs,” said one participant. “Now I can run longer, and I feel proud of myself.”

Still, community-based programs like FitWit Foundation may offer something many teens need: encouragement, structure and a sense of belonging.

“Kids don’t need another lecture,” said a FitWit Foundation coach. “They need people who believe in them, who make fitness fun, and who teach them skills they can use for life.”

The CDC says preventing childhood obesity requires support at every level — families, schools, health care providers and communities. Programs that combine physical activity, nutrition education and positive mentorship may be one way to help young people build healthier habits early.

But in Atlanta, one youth fitness program is making a different case: the most meaningful gift a young person can receive may be a healthier body, stronger confidence and a lifelong understanding of how to care for themselves.

That idea is at the heart of the **FitWit Foundation**, an Atlanta-based nonprofit that uses fitness, nutrition education and mentorship to help teens build healthier habits. Through its teen boot camp program, the foundation gives young people something that cannot be wrapped — endurance, discipline, self-confidence and a supportive community.

During a season often centered on excess, the program offers a timely reminder for parents, schools and donors: toys and gadgets may entertain children for a few weeks, but a healthy lifestyle can shape the rest of their lives.

### A Different Kind of Holiday Gift

Childhood and teen health remain major concerns across the country. Many young people spend long hours on screens, have limited access to safe recreation, and face barriers to fresh food, structured exercise and health education. For families dealing with financial pressure, transportation challenges or demanding work schedules, organized fitness opportunities can be especially difficult to access.

The FitWit Foundation’s teen boot camp aims to close that gap.

The program combines group workouts, coaching, nutrition lessons and personal goal-setting in a structured environment designed specifically for young people. Instead of focusing only on weight or athletic performance, the boot camp emphasizes effort, consistency, teamwork and practical skills teens can carry into adulthood.

Participants learn how to move safely, build strength, improve cardiovascular fitness and understand the connection between food, energy and long-term health. Just as importantly, they are surrounded by adults and peers who encourage them to keep showing up.

### Boot Camp With a Bigger Purpose

At a typical teen boot camp session, students might rotate through body-weight exercises, running drills, agility work, stretching and team-based challenges. Coaches stress proper form, persistence and mutual support. The tone is demanding but encouraging — less about competition and more about progress.

That approach is important for teenagers, many of whom may feel uncomfortable in traditional athletic settings. Not every teen plays school sports. Not every teen has a gym membership or a safe park nearby. FitWit’s model gives students a place to start, regardless of their fitness level.

The program also treats health as more than exercise. Nutrition education is woven into the experience, helping students understand hydration, balanced meals, portion sizes, healthy snacks and the effects of sugary drinks and highly processed foods. The goal is not to lecture teens, but to give them practical tools they can use at home, at school and later in life.

These outcomes matter because they reflect more than short-term fitness gains. They point to behavior change — the kind of change that can affect how young people manage stress, approach food, use their free time and view their own abilities.

### Why Health May Outlast Holiday Toys

Holiday gifts often lose their appeal quickly. A toy breaks. A gadget becomes outdated. A child outgrows a trend. But the lessons learned through fitness — how to set a goal, work through discomfort, recover from setbacks and celebrate progress — can stay with a young person for years.

That is especially valuable during adolescence, when habits often become patterns. A teen who learns to enjoy movement is more likely to stay active as an adult. A student who understands nutrition is better equipped to make choices in a cafeteria, convenience store or college dining hall. A young person who feels strong may also feel more confident in the classroom, at home and among peers.

The FitWit Foundation’s program also reframes health as something communal. Teens are not simply told to “exercise more.” They are invited into a team. They are coached, encouraged and held accountable. For many students, that support can make the difference between quitting and continuing.

### A Gift for Families, Too

A youth fitness program can also have ripple effects at home. When teens learn healthier habits, they often bring that knowledge back to their families. A student may ask for more water instead of soda, suggest a walk after dinner, help prepare a healthier meal or encourage a sibling to be active.

In that sense, the gift of a healthy lifestyle is not only for one child. It can influence an entire household.

For parents looking beyond traditional presents this holiday season, options might include sports equipment, cooking classes, family fitness memberships, outdoor experiences or enrollment in programs like FitWit’s teen boot camp. For donors, supporting youth wellness programs can be a way to give children access to opportunities they might not otherwise have.

### Investing in the Future

The holiday season often invites reflection on what children truly need. Entertainment has its place, and there is nothing wrong with the joy of opening a toy or gadget. But Atlanta’s FitWit Foundation offers a broader vision of giving — one rooted in health, confidence and opportunity.

A boot camp may not look like a conventional holiday present. It does not come with wrapping paper or batteries. But for a teenager who discovers strength, endurance and self-belief, it may be one of the most lasting gifts of all.

This year, the healthiest gift for a child might be the chance to move, learn, grow and believe that taking care of themselves is worth the effort.
